credit: Three projectile tiles and the title scenery from Kenney Tower Defense (Top-Down), CC0. See public/assets/kenney/License.txt. Everything else the game draws is original art.
note: Every sprite the game draws is named here. `files` maps a key to a path under assetRoot, so a new art pack is a path change. `render` gives a key its anchor and on-screen height, so art of any source size drops in without touching code.

hud-peanut._note: THE PEANUT, on its own, painted. It was in public/assets/ui_icons/ the whole time and art.json never named it, so every peanut in the game was drawn either as part of the counter plate or as `gen-icon-peanut` -- a flood-filled cut-out of that plate, which is the plain white peanut the HUD was showing.
hud-peanut._size: 512x512 IS THE CANVAS, NOT THE ART, and these are SOURCE EXTENTS that fitInBox divides by -- so the canvas figure made every peanut in the game 3% small and, worse, made a shape that is 1.25:1 behave as though it were square. Measured ink is 498x400; run `python3 tools/measure_art.py` and read the UI icons section to re-derive it.

hud-peanuts._field: AUTHORED, NOT MEASURED, and the only one of the three that is. fieldLeft is where the number starts, and dark_field in measure_art.py finds it as the first column of the plate's longest dark run -- which on the other two plates lands just past the painted icon. This plate no longer HAS a painted icon (see _icon), so the same measurement would return the field's own left edge, 0.0647, and print the counter over the peanut. 0.319 is the wave plate's, measured on the identical 232x96 frame, so all three numbers start in the same place.
hud-peanuts._icon: THE PAINTED PEANUT IS GONE FROM THE PLATE. It was a plain white outline from before the game had peanut art, and HudScene draws the real one over that end -- so the chip showed two peanuts, the white one poking out from behind the brown one. No draw call made it: it was in the picture. tools/clear_peanut_plate.py flattened that end back to the field colour.

ui-cake._note: THE CAKE A LEVEL PAYS OUT, one file for both states. Earned is the picture; unearned is built at runtime by systems/Desaturate.ts -- greyscaled, pulled towards light grey and faded, never DARKENED, because the frosting is dark chocolate and darkening it makes it vanish against the dark HUD. Two files would have been the mistake the placeholder ability icons made: the word LOCKED was painted into the art, so an available button looked locked and no draw call could say otherwise.
ui-cake._size: 1024x1024 IS THE CANVAS. These are SOURCE INK EXTENTS, which is what fitInBox divides by -- `python3 tools/measure_art.py`, the UI icons section, re-derives them. 1024 is the right source size for a 96px largest display under the >=7x rule in CLAUDE.md, and at webp q95 it costs 122KB of a 40MB budget.

fx-eli-fire._note: RUSSINGA IS FIRE, the second held beam. TWELVE 381x330 cells in ONE ROW, and it MUST NOT BE RE-SLICED OR RE-GRIDDED: the export was a 4x3 grid whose frames each had their muzzle somewhere different, drifting 51px across and 151px down, and it was flattened to a row with every muzzle registered on one point before it reached the repository. Re-gridding it puts the drift back.
fx-eli-fire._anchor: THE MUZZLE, as a fraction of the cell. anchorX 0.0814 is x31.0 of 381, which sits inside the ink of all twelve frames and 13-21px in from each one's left edge -- the fire starts at the hand and its glow spills back behind it, exactly as fx-mind-laser's does. anchorY is the CORE'S CENTRE LINE over the sustain frames, which is what tools/measure_art.py's beam-strip section measures: it reads 0.5955, against the 0.5909 the brief proposed, and the measurement is what is recorded. Re-run that section after any re-export.
fx-eli-fire._content: contentWidth IS NOT THE CELL. `GameScene.aimHeld` scales the sprite by `range / contentWidth`, and the sprite's origin is the muzzle -- so this has to be the distance from the muzzle to the PAINTED TIP if the fire is to end where the damage corridor ends. The union ink runs x10-370, so that is 370 - 31 = 339. fx-mind-laser records 225, its whole cell, and gets away with it only because its muzzle is at x0 and its ink reaches x224: the two coincide there and do not here. contentHeight is the union ink height, y10-316.
fx-eli-fire._beamCoreHeight: THE PAINTED CORE, not the cell, and this is the number fx-mind-laser shipped wrong. `beamWidth` describes the corridor that is DAMAGED, so dividing it by the 330px cell -- most of which is muzzle glow and rolling smoke -- squeezes a 108px flame into a fifth of its drawn thickness and flattens every highlight into a gradient. Measured over the sustain frames by tools/measure_art.py. At range 420 and beamWidth 72 the scales are 1.24 across and 0.67 down, an anisotropy of 1.86:1 against the laser's 3.14:1.

enemy-intern._note: MEASURED BY tools/measure_art.py, like the whole level 8 cast, and none of it typed by hand. `contentWidth`/`contentHeight` are SOURCE extents and `fitInBox` divides by them, so they go stale silently on a re-export -- re-run the script and copy them back; `displayHeight` is in world pixels and survives a re-export untouched. THE INTERN'S BOX IS WIDER THAN HE IS TALL, 854x567, because loose paper flies out behind him. His 58 is 58 of ROBOT: the robot's own ink fills the canvas height and only the paper adds width. His anchorX of 0.7242 is his ONE PLANTED FOOT rather than the middle of the picture -- he is running -- and his foot band is 0.88, the shallowest cut that finds the foot and not the litter, which is the opposite of every other band in the file and is explained there.

enemy-hr._note: HER FOOT BAND IS 0.97, the deepest in tools/measure_art.py, and the Consultant's is 0.96. Both are drawn mid-stride with a very long gait and their two contact patches span nearly the whole canvas -- her trailing foot is at x17 of 628 and her leading one reaches the right edge -- so a shallower band measures a footprint 92% of her width and manifest.test.ts rejects that at 85%. Nothing was swallowed; the stance is that wide. The deeper cut measures the contact patches rather than the ankles.

enemy-office-drone._note: LANDSCAPE, 4084x2888, and it HOVERS -- so its shadow and its x anchor both come off the ink rather than off a stance, which is the rule the Zamboni, the Glitch Bug, the Glider and the Rooster already get. It is a GROUND unit for every other purpose: every tower can shoot it. See the `_layer` note on its enemies.json row.

enemy-ceo._note: RENDERED FLUSH TO HIS CANVAS: the source outline is shaved by 40 to 76 px on each side and the file has been PADDED 80 px all round to give the sprite room. The shaved pixels are gone from the art and are not recoverable, so anchorY is 0.9812 rather than 1.0 -- the padding is transparent and the anchor has to sit on the ink.

fx-performance-scan._note: AN 8-FRAME HORIZONTAL SHEET ON A UNIFORM GRID, 272x610 per cell, with clean alpha -- it arrived cut and is not re-sliced here. `registerEffectAnims` builds one animation per manifest entry carrying a `sheet`, so declaring the grid is the whole of wiring it up, and `forgetEffectAnims` drops that animation when the texture is freed by asking the TEXTURE which animations were cut from it. See reports/2026-09-10-the-null-frame.md for what happens to an effect animation that outlives its texture.

fx-performance-buff._note: ONE FRAME, NOT A SHEET, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: the buff marker hangs over a reviewed enemy for the rest of its life, and a marker that animates forever is one more thing drawing every frame on a phone. Carrying no `sheet` means `registerEffectAnims` never builds an animation for it, so there is none to outlive the texture. It is still level art and is still freed with the level. Anchored at its BASE, like `fx-mind-control`, because `GameScene.syncStatusMarkers` sits a marker just clear of the top of the sprite it belongs to.

enemy-hatchback._note: LANDSCAPE, 692x389 (1.78:1). A car's shadow is the car, so shadowWidth is the whole body and anchorX is its ink centre -- see tools/measure_art.py. RULE 7: wants 469 px of source for a 66 px sprite and has 389 (0.83x). SHORT, and the shortfall is in the art rather than in the number: 66 world px is the smallest vehicle on the board and dropping it further would make a car narrower than the lane markings it drives over.

enemy-musclecar._note: LANDSCAPE, 647x394 (1.64:1). RULE 7: wants 526 px and has 394 (0.75x). SHORT.

enemy-van._note: LANDSCAPE, 837x641 (1.31:1). THE ONLY ONE OF THE NINE THAT MEETS RULE 7: wants 626 px of source for an 86 px sprite and has 641 (1.05x). displayHeight is 86 rather than the brief's 88 because the shortest tower is 87.1 world px and tests/content.test.ts holds the rank and file under it.

enemy-bladerig._note: LANDSCAPE, 1147x497, and at 2.31:1 it is the widest thing in the manifest. At displayHeight 130 it draws 300 world px across -- wider than any tower's reach is deep, which is the mini boss reading as unstoppable before it does anything. RULE 7: wants 924 px of source and has 497 (0.54x). SHORT by nearly half.

enemy-transporter._note: LANDSCAPE, 1033x495 (2.09:1), and at displayHeight 175 it is the largest sprite in the game -- 365 world px across, 28.5% of the canvas. RULE 7: wants 1244 px of source and has 495 (0.40x), THE WORST RATIO IN THE FILE. A re-export at 1244 px tall is the only thing that fixes it; nothing in the manifest can. Its four cargo cars are painted on the trailer and are the four `enemy-cargo-*` sprites below, which is what makes the finale legible.

enemy-cargo-red._note: LANDSCAPE, 401x213 (1.88:1). One of the four cars on the transporter's trailer. RULE 7: wants 512 px and has 213 (0.42x). SHORT.

enemy-cargo-blue._note: LANDSCAPE, 397x254 (1.56:1). RULE 7: wants 512 px and has 254 (0.50x). SHORT.

enemy-cargo-yellow._note: LANDSCAPE, 360x216 (1.67:1). RULE 7: wants 512 px and has 216 (0.42x). SHORT.

enemy-cargo-green._note: LANDSCAPE, 384x253 (1.52:1). RULE 7: wants 512 px and has 253 (0.49x). SHORT.

levelArt._note: ART THAT ONLY EXISTS INSIDE A LEVEL, and so is not loaded at boot. The plates went first (see `map` above and reports/2026-09-07-the-crash.md); this is the rest of the same argument. Every key here is fetched when a level starts and given back when it ends, exactly as a plate is, which took 90.8 MB of enemies, effects, signs, soldiers and in-play buttons off the title screen. THE ENEMIES ARE NOT LISTED HERE and that is deliberate: enemies.json already says which sprite each enemy wears and the wave tables already say which enemies a level fields, so the set is COMPUTED per level rather than written down twice -- systems/LevelArt.ts. A level loads its own enemies and nobody else's. What is left in `shared` is art any level might need: the effects, the props, the soldiers, the projectiles and the two in-play panels. THE DEFAULT IS BOOT. A new key that nobody adds here stays in the boot manifest, which costs memory and cannot break a screen; a menu key listed here by mistake would be a missing texture on a menu, which can. tests/levelart.test.ts checks the direction that matters -- that every enemy sprite and every ability effect is level art, and that nothing a menu draws is.
levelArt._notDecor: THE DECOR IS NOT HERE, and it is the one that looks like it should be. `decor-bush` and its five siblings are Kenney tiles scattered on the board -- and TitleScene.decorateBackdrop scatters twenty-six of them behind the title as well, at alpha 0.12. Listing them would have put magenta squares on the first screen of the game. They are 24 KB between them, so nothing is lost by leaving them at boot; what would have been lost is the first screen. Measured, not assumed: the audit that found them is in reports/2026-09-08-the-memory-numbers.md.
levelArt._notTowers: THE TOWER BASE SPRITES ARE NOT HERE EITHER. The loadout deals a hand of tower cards and draws each one's `sprite` from towers.json, so `turret-ledger` and the rest are menu art whether or not a level is running. Only the TIER art is level-only: `tierSprite` swaps a tower's silhouette as it upgrades and nothing outside a run ever calls it. Same for the hero roster -- every hero, powered and not, is on the loadout picker.
levelArt._notAbilityIcons: `ability-*` ARE NOT HERE. They are 256px icons on the loadout cards and in the HUD's ability rail, 0.25 MB each; the EFFECT each ability plays is what moved, and those are the `fx-*` above.
levelArt._level10:
LEVEL 10'S ART, LANDED AHEAD OF LEVEL 10. Every key in this row is on disk, measured and registered, and NOTHING DRAWS ANY OF IT: level 10 has no row in levels.json, no roster in enemies.json and no tower in towers.json, so `levelArtKeys` never resolves the id and `orphanedLevelArt` names all twenty-one of them plus `map-level10`. That list in tests/levelart.test.ts is the register of what is WAITING, and it empties itself the day level 10 gets its row -- the same way level 6's five entries, level 7's and 8's eight, and the fourteen machine tower skins each left it.
WHY THE ROW EXISTS AT ALL RATHER THAN LEAVING THE KEYS AT BOOT: a key that is not level art is queued by `queueArt` on every boot by every player, so twenty-one unused textures would be about 5.4 MB on the loading bar for art no board can show. Filed here they cost nothing anywhere -- not at boot, and not on levels 1 to 9, because no level asks for them.
`map-level10` IS NOT IN THIS LIST and does not need to be: it is in `map` above, which makes it a PLATE_KEY, which is already level art. `level10` JOINS `towerSkins.machine.levels` THE DAY IT GETS A ROW and not before, for the reason written there.
THE THREE LEVEL 10 COMIC PANELS AND THE TITLE CARD ARE CONVERTED AND ARE DELIBERATELY NOT NAMED HERE. Comic panels have never been in this manifest -- cutscenes.json owns them -- and naming one here fails tests/manifest.test.ts twice over: `cutscenes` becomes an asset directory that systems/Cutscenes.ts names as a string literal, and a panel is bound to no role that draws it. They sit under public/assets/cutscenes/ waiting for a row in cutscenes.json, which cannot be written until level 10 is a level. See reports/2026-09-14-level-10-assets.md.
levelArt._byLevel:
ART ONE LEVEL DRAWS AND NO OTHER, keyed by level id. `shared` above is every level's bill; this is one level's. Level 9 brings seven effect sheets, four build-node variants and a screen -- 3.6 MB, more than any plate -- and none of it means anything on levels 1 to 8. A key here is level art (so boot never queues it) and is loaded by exactly the level named. The same shape `towerSkins` already uses, and the reason LevelArt.ts reads both.
ENEMY-HAT-GTT-B IS IN THIS LIST AND HAD TO BE PUT THERE BY HAND, which is the one gap in the derivation above. `ENEMY_SPRITE_KEYS` is derived from enemies.json's `sprite` field, and the hat's alternate tilt is named by `regen.altSprite` instead -- so it was classified as ordinary art, downloaded at BOOT by every player on every level, and freed by nothing. 0.19 MB on the loading bar for a picture only level 9 can show. Found by diffing the boot path against main rather than by any test: `levelart.test.ts` checks that nothing in a level's list is missing, not that nothing missing from a list should be in it. Any future field that names a second sprite for an enemy needs a row here too.

counterIcon._note: WHERE AN ICON DRAWN OVER A COUNTER PLATE GOES, taken off the heart that is painted into the lives plate so a drawn icon and a painted one sit the same. The heart's ink measures x21-74, y24-76 on a 229x96 plate (`python3 tools/measure_art.py`, the counter icon box section); these are those numbers as fractions of the plate's HEIGHT, which is the one dimension all three plates share (232x96, 229x96, 232x96). Only the peanuts plate uses them -- its icon is the one that is drawn rather than painted -- but they are the shared geometry rather than that plate's own, which is why they live beside `counters` and not in its render entry.

generated._peanutIcon: RETIRED. It was a flood-filled cut-out of the counter plate, generated at boot by src/systems/PeanutIcon.ts, and its own docstring said to delete it the day real peanut art arrived. The art was already in the repository; art.json simply never named it. `ui.peanutIcon` is the real file now.

hero._note: THE ROSTER AND NOTHING ELSE. This section used to carry Cory's own frame lists as well -- `idle`, `walk`, `attack` and their per-set anchors -- because he was the only hero and his walk sheet was the animation system. All five heroes are single pictures now, so the lists are gone with the sheet and `roster` is the whole of it. `attackImpactFrame` stays: the swing still lands on a frame of a clock even though nothing swaps a texture on it, and the damage timing is a tuned number.
hero._roster: EVERY HERO'S ART, in one place. `base` is how it starts, `powered` is what it wears once its health has been below half, and `walk`/`attack` are its frame lists or null. NULL IS THE INTERESTING CASE: a hero with no walk sheet is a single picture that would slide across the field, so Hero.ts gives it a small procedural bob instead. Dropping a real sheet in later is replacing the null with a frame list here -- the bob turns itself off, because it is conditioned on the sheet being absent rather than on a flag someone has to remember.

worldMap._note: The world map screen, COMPOSED rather than painted. One tiling background reused at every size, one small card cropped from each level's own plate, and a trail drawn in code from the levels' mapPositions. Adding a level is a row in levels.json and one card here; no art is regenerated.

machine._levels: LEVEL 9 WEARS THE MACHINE SKIN, and this list is the switch. It was deliberately EMPTY from the day the fourteen files landed until now, because `levelArtKeys` resolves an unknown id to the default level and a skin switched on for a board that never loaded it is a missing texture on level 1. Level 9 has a row in levels.json now, so the id resolves and the skin is real: every tower and both of the Ima Dummy's lads are repainted as machine-world hardware on that board and on no other. Level 10 joins this list when it ships. THE 3.75 MB STOPS BEING RESIDENT NOWHERE and becomes a real download for whoever opens level 9 -- which is what tests/content.test.ts's per-level cap now measures.

_towerSkins:
A WHOLE-BOARD RESKIN OF THE TOWERS, chosen by which level is running. `keys` maps the ordinary manifest key to the skinned one; `levels` is the list of level ids that wear the skin, and IT IS THE ONLY SWITCH. Everything else -- the loadout, the tower drawer, the world map, every menu -- asks for the ordinary key and is untouched by this, which is why the skin is resolved at the two places a tower's BODY art is chosen (entities/Tower.ts's wearTier and GameScene's soldier) and nowhere else.
WHY `levels` WAS EMPTY UNTIL LEVEL 9, and the reason is a trap worth keeping written down. The machine art was committed for levels 9 and 10 before either existed, and naming `level9` here then would not have loaded it -- `levelArtKeys` resolves an unknown id to the DEFAULT level, so the switch would have looked wired and done nothing, or worse, asked level 1 for fourteen textures it never fetched. Level 9 has a row in levels.json now, so the id resolves and the skin is real. `level10` joins the list on the day level 10 gets its row and not before.
THE KEYS DO NOT MATCH THE FILENAMES and two of them actively mislead: `turret-extension` is tower_filing and `turret-shelter` is tower_tax. Read the pairing off `files`, never off a filename.
EVERY SKINNED KEY IS LEVEL ART, so boot loads none of it -- systems/LevelArt.ts adds a level's skin keys only when that level is in `levels`, and GameScene.freeLevelArt gives them back through the same path that forgets their animations. 14 more textures cost 0 MB at boot and 0 MB on any level not in this list.
_towerSkinsRender:
WHY EACH SKINNED KEY HAS ITS OWN `render` ENTRY, copied rather than shared. `applyRender` scales by `displayHeight / sprite.height` -- the CANVAS height -- and anchors on `anchorY`, so a key with no render entry falls back to {anchorX: 0.5, anchorY: 0.5} with no height at all: the tower would draw at its source size, centre-anchored, half-buried in its own pad. Every machine file has the same canvas as its original, so `anchorX`, `anchorY`, `displayHeight` and `shadowWidth` are COPIED from it and reproduce its placement and scale exactly. `contentWidth`/`contentHeight` are the machine file's OWN measured ink, because `fitInBox` divides by those (CLAUDE.md rule 7) and the ink is not the same.
ONE PAIR DISAGREES: tower_withholding_t2_machine's ink starts at y=67 in a 215x371 frame against the original's y=0, so 304 source px of ink against 371. Its base is still flush with the canvas bottom, so it sits on its pad correctly and needs no offset -- but the copied displayHeight of 107.7 puts 88.3 px of tower on screen where the original puts 107.7, which is 1.2 px taller than the tier-1 machine and reads as no growth at all on the upgrade. That is an art fix, not a metadata one: raising displayHeight to 131.4 would land the height and widen the base 20% past the pad. See reports/2026-09-13-machine-tower-skins.md.
_optional: Art that may legitimately be absent. A key here is skipped by the loader with a console warning rather than a missing-texture error, and every one belongs to a family with a named fallback -- tests/boot.test.ts enforces that. IT IS NOT A LICENCE TO SHIP WITHOUT THE FILE. `queueArt` requests every key in `files`, optional or not -- it cannot know which are absent without asking the server -- so a listed key whose file is missing is a 404 on every boot for every player, and three of them shipped that way. tests/assets.test.ts now fails on exactly that. The eight icons left here are the tower-panel glyphs, which have a generated stand-in.
_greyable: A greyscale copy is built for each of these at boot (BootScene, systems/Desaturate.ts) and the HUD swaps to it when the thing is unavailable. EVERY HERO ABILITY ICON IS HERE BECAUSE OF THE POWERED-FORM GATE. An ability with `poweredOnly` is greyed out until the hero transforms, and a tint cannot say that -- Phaser's tint multiplies, so a tinted icon reads as "in shadow" rather than as "switched off". It used to read as neither: the key was absent from this list, `greyKey` named a texture that had never been built, the swap was skipped and the button kept its full colour with only a dim tint on it. The word LOCKED being painted into the placeholder art was what made that survivable, and that word is gone with the placeholders.
_fx: EFFECTS THE GAME DRAWS FOR ITSELF, by role. `spark`, `blast`, `puff` and `muzzle` are combat feedback; `bossBolt` is one boss's projectile; `stunned`, `burn` and `mindControl` are STATUS MARKERS drawn over an enemy for as long as the status lasts, which is why they are here rather than in heroes.json beside the ability that applied them -- a burn is a fact about the enemy, and anything that can set something alight draws the same flame. `mindControl` is live now: Courtland's Mind Control sets `Enemy.controlled` and `enemyMarker` in GameScene draws this over every enemy it turns, which is what keeps two enemies fighting each other from reading as a bug.
_heroHeight: WHY hero-cory-power CARRIES NO displayHeight. Every other sprite's on-screen height is a manifest field, and CLAUDE.md rule 7 says so. The Rivian is the exception because its height is a decision about ONE HERO rather than about one picture: it is 1.51:1, so at the roster's height it would be wider than the road, and the number that fixes that belongs beside the hero it is about. `heroes.json cory.poweredHeight` is it, and it is the only copy -- a second one here is how the two come to disagree. Hero.ts asks the roster first and falls back to this entry, so a hero with no `poweredHeight` is sized by its art exactly as before, and tests/heroes.test.ts fails if a powered form has a height from neither.
_markers: THE SPAWN AND EXIT BADGES, and they are SHARED level art rather than any one level's: every level draws them, derived from its own lane waypoints by systems/Markers.ts. contentWidth/contentHeight are the INK extents from tools/measure_art.py and on these four they happen to equal the canvas -- the artwork reaches every edge, there is no transparent margin -- which is a MEASUREMENT rather than an assumption. Recorded because the usual failure is the opposite: hud-peanut shipped 512x512 against a 498x400 painting and drew 3% small forever.
